# Manufacturing Technology Options for Hollow Motor Shafts in NEV Electric Drive Units

For most high-volume steel hollow motor shafts in New Energy Vehicle (NEV) electric drive units, the strongest default is a near-net cold, warm, or semi-hot forging route followed by precision machining, heat treatment, grinding, balancing, and inspection. A simple, repeatable shaft favors cold or warm forging, extrusion, or tube-based rotary swaging. A bottle-shaped or stepped monobloc shaft with a demanding internal contour favors semi-hot mandrel radial forging; a thin-walled tubular shaft with integrated splines or helical features favors rotary swaging combined with axial forming or spline rolling. No single process can be ranked as universally cheapest or strongest because the supplied evidence contains no common geometry, volume, fatigue, balance, cycle-time, and cost comparison across all routes.

The practical material baseline is alloy or case-hardening steel—especially 42CrMo4/4140, 20MnCr5/20CrMnTi, 20CrNiMo, or, for higher duty, 4340 or 18CrNiMo7-6. Aluminum, titanium, magnesium, copper, stainless steel, and nickel alloys are technically formable through several route families, but the available evidence does not establish them as generally qualified substitutes for high-volume NEV traction-motor shafts. For prototypes and low-volume programs, machining from tube or bar remains the most flexible fallback.

## Roadmap and assessment method

The report first defines the shaft’s operating envelope and the requirements that make the application different from an ordinary industrial motor shaft. It then catalogs the current forming families, separating established automotive practice from technically demonstrated, conditional, and emerging routes.

The comparison addresses four practical questions:

1. Which materials and heat treatments can each process accommodate?
2. How do tooling, capital, cycle time, material utilization, automation, and production volume affect cost-effectiveness?
3. What machining, spline or gear formation, heat treatment, balancing, and inspection remain after forming?
4. Which routes best fit high-volume NEV shafts, and under what geometry, material, and volume conditions should an alternative be selected?

The recommendation is intentionally conditional. The available evidence includes industrial production descriptions, supplier data, standards, simulations, laboratory studies, and analogues such as automotive axle sleeves and transmission shafts. These sources establish process mechanisms and commercial plausibility, but they do not provide one validated head-to-head ranking for a single NEV shaft design.

## 1. Application requirements for an NEV hollow motor shaft

### 1.1 Functional role in the electric drive unit

A rotor shaft is the mechanical link between the electric motor and the reduction gear or final drivetrain. It supports the rotor stack and, depending on motor architecture, permanent magnets, excitation-winding supports, balancing disks, slip-ring or induction components, and bearing locations. In a permanent-magnet synchronous motor (PMSM), the shaft carries the laminated rotor and magnets; in an electrically excited synchronous motor (EESM), it also supports star-shaped disks and field windings; in an asynchronous machine (ASM), it supports the steel core and conductive cage or bars. These arrangements are described in the [Hirschvogel rotor-shaft paper](https://www.hirschvogel.com/fileadmin/user_upload/ATZlive_Paper_HIVO_Rotorshaft_klf_V6.pdf).

The shaft performs several functions simultaneously:

- transmits continuous and transient torque to the gearbox;
- carries bending loads created by rotor mass, gear forces, bearing reactions, and assembly;
- maintains the rotor stack and bearing seats on a common axis;
- transmits torque through internal or external splines, a helical gear, or another formed interface;
- withstands repeated acceleration, deceleration, and regenerative-braking reversals;
- maintains dimensional stability at high rotational speed;
- reduces mass and polar inertia through the hollow section;
- sometimes provides an oil, coolant, wiring, or lubricant passage.

A hollow shaft is therefore not simply a lighter solid shaft. The bore changes torsional stiffness, bending stiffness, local buckling resistance, thermal behavior, wall-thickness sensitivity, and the way manufacturing defects are distributed.

Zhang et al. describe an electric-motor shaft as carrying tension, compression, bending, and torsional loads. Their design discussion also places the first critical speed above the operating speed, with a design target approximately 20–25% higher than operating speed in the cited rotor-attached shaft case [Zhang et al., 2018](https://publica.fraunhofer.de/bitstreams/a343908c-8dd5-4ed6-bcbf-366b0a2a9d09/download).

Regenerative braking adds an important load-direction issue. A vehicle-drive-shaft patent distinguishes mainly one-directional torsion in a conventional internal-combustion drivetrain from forward and reverse torque application in hybrid and electric vehicles during traction and regenerative braking [US20160305469A1](https://patents.google.com/patent/US20160305469A1/en). That patent concerns a vehicle drive shaft rather than a motor rotor shaft, so its load magnitudes and geometry should not be transferred directly. Its mechanism is nevertheless relevant: a shaft designed for repeated torque reversals must be assessed for bidirectional torsional fatigue, spline contact, weld or interface integrity, and residual-stress effects.

### 1.2 Representative geometry

A useful screening envelope, rather than a universal specification, is:

- outside diameter: approximately 40–70 mm;
- wall thickness: approximately 4–6 mm;
- overall shaft length: approximately 200–350 mm;
- two precision bearing sections;
- one or more splines, a gear, or an end-forming feature;
- optional stepped or bottle-shaped inner contour;
- possible internal oil or coolant passage.

These ranges come from professional manufacturing experience summarized by Fink. The same source reports general outer-diameter tolerances of approximately 14–20 μm, bearing-section outer-diameter tolerances of 7–12 μm over the bearing length, and bearing cylindricity of 5–8 μm for high-speed rotor shafts [Hirschvogel rotor-shaft paper](https://www.hirschvogel.com/fileadmin/user_upload/ATZlive_Paper_HIVO_Rotorshaft_klf_V6.pdf). They should be treated as representative production ranges, not as a substitute for a program drawing.

A separate Chinese design study gives a smaller 10 kW example: a 20CrMnTi hollow gear shaft with a 27 mm inner diameter, 33–60 mm outer diameter, 80–250 mm length, 28 Nm peak torque, and 12,000 rpm [Zhang et al., 2018](https://publica.fraunhofer.de/bitstreams/a343908c-8dd5-4ed6-bcbf-366b0a2a9d09/download). That case demonstrates that the product family covers more than one size class; it is not a universal NEV specification.

The [FITGEN e-axle report](https://www.fitgen-project.eu/files/FITGEN_D1.3_Reliable%20and%20scalable%20design%20ready%20for%20mass%20manufacturing%20and%20dismantling.pdf) describes a reference rotor operating in the 20,000–22,000 rpm range after exceeding an 18,000 rpm project target. It is useful for high-speed screening, but it does not provide the shaft drawing, wall thickness, balance grade, or shaft-level runout requirements.

### 1.3 Why the hollow section is valuable—and where it becomes dangerous

For a thin-walled circular shaft, the polar second moment is:

\[
J=\frac{\pi}{32}(D_o^4-D_i^4),\quad \tau_{\max}=\frac{16TD_o}{\pi(D_o^4-D_i^4)}
\]

where \(D_o\) is outside diameter, \(D_i\) is inside diameter, \(T\) is torque, and \(\tau_{\max}\) is the nominal maximum torsional shear stress.

For equal outside diameter and length, the mass ratio of a hollow shaft to a solid shaft is approximately:

\[
\frac{m_h}{m_s}=1-\left(\frac{D_i}{D_o}\right)^2
\]

The hollow section removes material near the neutral core, so mass can fall substantially while much of the torsional section modulus remains. However, the stiffness and strength penalties accelerate as the wall becomes thin, particularly under combined torsion and bending.

JEC reports that its 2024–2026 dataset of 22 EV traction-motor shaft programs found 30–40% mass reduction when solid 4140 was replaced by hollow 4140, with no measurable fatigue-life penalty in the tested continuous-duty context when the wall remained above 25% of outside diameter. The same source describes approximately 35% wall as a typical choice, 25% as a lower-margin limit requiring fatigue testing, and 50% as an excessive mass-saving target with a large fatigue penalty [JEC EV shaft requirements](https://www.motor-shaft.com/news/ev-motor-shaft-requirements-high-speed-high-torque-and-lightweight-design-challenges/). Because the source does not define the wall-thickness convention in a way that can be reconciled with every shaft drawing, this threshold must remain a screening rule rather than a general design law.

An illustrative calculation shows the trade-off. If a hypothetical shaft has \(D_o=50\) mm and a 5 mm radial wall, then \(D_i=40\) mm. The material cross-sectional area is 36% lower than that of a solid 50 mm shaft, while the ideal polar stiffness is about 59% of the solid value. This calculation is only geometric; it does not include bearing span, stress concentrations, rotor mass, critical speed, fatigue notch effects, or manufacturing defects.

The hollow section may also be used as a functional passage. Fink describes internal cooling for weight reduction, rotor cooling, and oil transport to the gearbox, with cleanliness requirements for gravimetric contamination and particle size. Gai’s thesis analyzes forced coolant flow through a hollow automotive traction-motor shaft and warns that shaft rotation creates secondary flow, making a stationary-shaft heat-transfer correlation invalid [Gai, 2020](https://theses.ncl.ac.uk/jspui/bitstream/10443/5024/1/Gai%20Y%202020.pdf). The FITGEN reference unit specifies 6–10 l/min of a 50/50 water-glycol mixture around the stator, but that is not evidence of a shaft-integrated cooling passage [FITGEN D1.3](https://www.fitgen-project.eu/files/FITGEN_D1.3_Reliable%20and%20scalable%20design%20ready%20for%20mass%20manufacturing%20and%20dismantling.pdf).

### 1.4 Speed, critical speed, balance, and runout

The shaft must remain dynamically stable over the complete operating range, including acceleration through resonances and high-speed operation above the first critical speed where the design permits supercritical running.

Available speed figures describe different application classes:

| Evidence or application class | Reported speed range or criterion | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---|
| JEC field dataset | 12,000–20,000 rpm continuous; 18,000–24,000 rpm typical first critical speed | Supplier-reported production-program range |
| FITGEN reference e-axle | 20,000–22,000 rpm rotor speed | High-speed project reference |
| Fink industrial experience | 20,000–30,000 rpm maximum speed | High-speed rotor-shaft envelope |
| Zhang et al. | Critical speed 20–25% above operating speed | Design rule in one electric-motor case |
| IMARC e-axle facility | 18,000 rpm dynamometer capability | Facility test envelope, not shaft specification |

The differences are not necessarily contradictory. Critical speed depends on shaft diameter and length, bearing span, rotor mass distribution, housing stiffness, and the location of gears, laminations, and balancing disks. The [JEC field guide](https://www.motor-shaft.com/news/ev-motor-shaft-requirements-high-speed-high-torque-and-lightweight-design-challenges/) emphasizes that the first bending frequency is a shaft-and-bearing-system property, not solely a material-strength property.

Balance grade must also be assigned to the complete rotor system and test speed. JEC reports G2.5 at rated speed and possible G1.0 requirements for permanent-magnet motors above 15,000 rpm. General industrial guidance maps G6.3 to ordinary electric motors and G2.5 to medium and large motors, while noting that tighter grades require more balancing runs [Lütgert balancing guidance](https://www.luetgert-antriebe.de/luetgert-neu-en/competences/mechanical-processing/balancing-according-to-din-iso-21940.php). These are application recommendations, not one universal hollow-shaft grade.

ISO 1940-1:2003 specified residual-unbalance tolerances and verification methods for rigid rotors, but that edition is withdrawn and was revised by ISO 21940-11:2016. ISO 21940-21:2022 addresses acceptance testing of balancing machines and emphasizes rotor-specific calibration at a defined mass and speed [ISO 1940-1](https://www.iso.org/standard/27092.html); [ANSI summary of ISO 21940-21:2022](https://blog.ansi.org/ansi/iso-21940-21-mechanical-vibration-rotor-balancing/). A production drawing should therefore specify the applicable current standard, residual unbalance, correction planes, balancing speed, and whether the requirement applies to the shaft, rotor subassembly, or complete motor.

### 1.5 Material and volume assumptions

Official and industrial NEV shaft specifications support a steel-centered assessment. T/ZJDJ 002-2022 preferentially lists 20CrMnTi, 20CrNiMo, 40Cr, and 42CrMo, together with the corresponding “H” grades under Chinese standards [T/ZJDJ 002-2022](https://ndls.cnis.ac.cn/standard/detail/1bf70fee23d908c4df27c754520158da). The 2026 T/CMEEEA 069 listing explicitly covers both solid and hollow motor shafts in pure-electric and plug-in-hybrid drive-motor systems [T/CMEEEA 069-2026](https://ndls.cnis.ac.cn/standard/detail/d5869705e3643a28e922abd0e5e14660). T/CAAMTB 265-2025 addresses hollow split-structure shafts press-fitted at room temperature, showing that split hollow architectures are now recognized in an NEV-specific manufacturing specification [T/CAAMTB 265-2025](https://ndls.cnis.ac.cn/standard/detail/e69a321a53a870b0b33c0d0ad403f82b).

There is no validated target-program specification combining shaft dimensions, torque spectrum, critical speed, wall thickness, balance, runout, fluid passage, heat-treatment distortion, and annual shaft volume. E-axle capacity should not be confused with shaft capacity: one facility case reports 240,000 integrated e-axles per year, expandable to 360,000, but does not state the number of hollow shafts produced [IMARC e-axle facility](https://www.imarcengineering.com/case-study/electric-motor-and-e-axle-manufacturing-facility).

Accordingly, the economic comparison below uses three qualitative volume situations:

- prototype or low volume: tooling amortization is weak and flexibility dominates;
- serial production: dedicated forming and automated machining begin to offset tooling;
- high volume: repeatability, cycle time, yield, automation, and amortized tooling dominate.

The supplied evidence does not support numerical unit costs or universal break-even quantities for a named NEV shaft. The FIA forging guide gives broad process indicators—impression-die forging is associated with 300 or more pieces typically, cold forging with usually more than 10,000, open-die forging with one or more and up to about 50 typical, and rolled rings with 10 or more typical—but these are general forging ranges, not shaft-specific break-even points [Forging Industry Association guide](https://www.forging.org/Common/Uploaded%20files/Design%20Engineering%20Center/Product%20Design%20Guide%20for%20Forging.pdf).

## 2. Current forming-technology landscape

### 2.1 Process inventory and maturity

The following inventory covers the forming families that can produce a hollow shaft, a hollow near-net preform, or a shaft-integrated feature. A complete production route normally combines more than one family.

| Named technique | Hollow output or preform | Maturity for NEV shafts | Suitable scale | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-die and mandrel forging | Large hollow shell, tube, stepped bore, or prototype preform | Established forging technology; niche for small NEV shafts | Prototype, low volume, large or unusual geometry | Low precision and substantial machining |
| Hot, warm, or cold impression-die forging | Solid or hollow near-net shaft, flanges, end forms, splines | Established automotive forming family; direct EV evidence is industrial but not fully quantified | Medium to very high volume | High tooling and force; bore and undercuts may need secondary work |
| Flashless, net-shape, and near-net forging | Close-to-final external features and selected holes or splines | Established in selected automotive components; shaft-specific qualification required | High volume | Tight billet-volume control and heat-treatment distortion |
| Upsetting, heading, and high-speed end forming | Enlarged ends, flanges, bearing bosses, local features | Established as a feature-forming operation | High volume for repeated end forms | Limited by unsupported length and buckling |
| Forward, backward, impact, and composite extrusion | Hollow cylinders, stepped bores, splines, gear or end features | Industrial for selected shaft features; direct NEV composite-extrusion evidence is mainly simulation | High volume for simple repeatable geometry | High forming loads, tool stress, formability and die life |
| Radial forging with mandrel | Stepped hollow monobloc, bottle-shaped shaft, internal contours | Strong automotive and supplier evidence; direct EV route is conditional | Serial to high volume | Tooling/process control, inner-hole distortion and damage |
| Rotary swaging | Thin-wall or variable-wall tube, external and internal reductions | Industrially relevant and directly promoted for rotor shafts; finished-shaft evidence remains limited | Serial to high volume | Friction, wall-thickness variation, multi-pass burden |
| Axial forming and spline extrusion | Internal splines, helical or axial features on hollow blank | Industrially established feature process | High volume | Requires run-out space or compatible profile |
| Spline rolling and helical-gear forming | External spline or helical feature on tube or shaft | Industrially evidenced | High volume | Runout, pitch error, tube deformation and tool loading |
| Cross-wedge or skew rolling | Stepped hollow preform or shaft section | Automotive rolling technology; hollow motor-shaft evidence is mainly simulation or analogue | Medium to high volume if qualified | Cavities, surface hollows, tool wear and machining allowance |
| Rotary compression or rotary forging | Stepped hollow shaft over mandrel | Laboratory demonstrated | Prototype to conditional serial | Limited production evidence and complex load control |
| Ring rolling | Seamless ring or annular flange preform | Established for rings; not normally a complete elongated motor shaft | Low to high volume for ring features | Does not directly create a complete rotor shaft |
| Seamless tube piercing, mandrel rolling, drawing, and sinking | Seamless hollow tube with controlled wall and bore | Established tube technology; direct motor-shaft qualification limited | Serial to high volume | Inner-surface defects, drawing/annealing and grinding burden |
| Flow forming, tube spinning, and rotary drawing | Tapered or stepped thin-wall tube | Technically established in other sectors; conditional for NEV shafts | Prototype to serial | Material and thermal control, multiple passes |
| Tube hydroforming and warm/hot gas forming | Stepped or contoured tube preform | Established in automotive structures; emerging for motor shafts | High volume only if geometry and capital justify it | High pressure, tooling, control complexity and cycle time |
| Friction-welded split or hybrid shaft | Nested tubes, forged ends, or separate flanges | Industrially plausible; NEV-specific standards cover split structures | Serial to high volume | Weld fatigue, runout, balance, inspection and assembly |
| Powder forging | Dense near-net symmetric component | Mature for selected automotive parts; weak hollow-shaft evidence | High volume | Hollow geometry, porosity control and limited shaft evidence |
| Additive manufacture | Direct hollow lattice or complex shaft | Emerging material capability but unqualified for production NEV shafts | Prototype or special low volume | Build rate, anisotropy, fatigue, balance, cost and post-processing |
| Machining from bar or tube | Finished shaft without bulk forming | Established fallback and prototype route | Prototype, low volume, changing variants | High chip volume, material waste, long cycle time |

This taxonomy reflects the distinction between a process that can shape the complete shaft and one that only creates a local feature. For example, Kinefac describes spline extrusion as a high-rate net-shape operation on a solid or hollow blank, but Fink’s production route still turns and drills the shaft before heat treatment. “Net shape” therefore applies to a profile or operation, not automatically to the whole motor shaft.

### 2.2 Historical transition in shaft manufacture

The principal transition has been from solid bar machining or welded assemblies toward near-net bulk forming, hollow tube forming, and integrated feature forming.

Machining from bar remains geometrically flexible, but the FIA guide notes that much of the purchased stock is removed as chips and that forged grain flow generally provides better material utilization and fatigue behavior. Fink’s cited internal global study reports that 95% of industrial rotor shafts in its surveyed population begin with a forging, while only 5% begin as bar or tube followed by machining [Hirschvogel rotor-shaft paper](https://www.hirschvogel.com/fileadmin/user_upload/ATZlive_Paper_HIVO_Rotorshaft_klf_V6.pdf). The survey’s sample and market definition are not disclosed, so the figure is an industrial indicator rather than a universal market statistic.

The second transition is from solid forgings to hollow, internally controlled preforms. Mandrels, radial forging, rotary swaging, extrusion, tube drawing, flow forming, and hydroforming are all attempts to place material where torque, bearing, spline, and assembly loads require it while removing material from the low-stress core.

The third transition is integration. Modern routes increasingly combine forming with axial spline forming, helical-gear forming, local hardening, and automated machining. Felss describes a six-station cold-forming chain that combines rotary swaging and axial forming from tube stock, while Profiroll describes NC-controlled rolling of a full-length involute spline on a thin-walled hollow rotor shaft [Felss rotor-shaft process chain](https://felss.com/en/blog/from-cost-factor-to-competitive-advantage-an-efficient-process-chain-for-rotor-shafts/); [Profiroll hollow rotor shaft](https://www.profiroll.com/fileadmin/user_upload/4_verfahren/5_Bibliothek/eMobility-Rotor_shaft.pdf).

The final transition is from fixed ICE-style high-volume lines to more adaptable production systems. Fink reports that short EV product lifecycles and volatile forecasts make capacity flexibility important, although flexibility usually increases production cost and time [Hirschvogel rotor-shaft paper](https://www.hirschvogel.com/fileadmin/user_upload/ATZlive_Paper_HIVO_Rotorshaft_klf_V6.pdf). That trade-off favors modular machining and adjustable forming systems when several shaft variants share equipment, while highly dedicated cold or impression-die tooling remains attractive for stable, very high-volume designs.

## 3. Detailed process profiles

### 3.1 Open-die, mandrel, and conventional bulk forging

#### Open-die and mandrel forging

Open-die forging works a heated billet between flat or simple-contour dies with repeated strokes and manipulation. For hollow workpieces, piercing, punching, trepanning, expanding, drawing, closing-in, and mandrel forging can be combined. A pierced or cupped billet is expanded or elongated over a mandrel while the wall is reduced and the length increased. The [Forging Industry Association guide](https://www.forging.org/Common/Uploaded%20files/Design%20Engineering%20Center/Product%20Design%20Guide%20for%20Forging.pdf) identifies hollow forging and mandrel operations as established open-die processes.

For a motor shaft, this route can produce a hollow cylindrical or stepped preform with strong directional flow. It is especially useful for prototypes, low-volume shafts, unusual internal contours, large diameters, or development work before production dies are committed. It has little special tooling cost and high geometry flexibility, but lower dimensional precision, longer handling time, and more finish machining than impression-die forging.

The process is therefore not the normal high-volume choice for a 40–70 mm, 200–350 mm passenger-vehicle rotor shaft. It remains useful for:

- early functional prototypes;
- pilot production before dedicated dies;
- low-volume performance variants;
- a fallback when the design changes frequently;
- large hollow shafts outside impression-die capability.

Mandrel forging can also be used as a preform for later radial forging, machining, or spline formation. Its main technical risks are inner-hole eccentricity, nonuniform wall reduction, local laps or folds, and distortion during subsequent heat treatment.

#### Impression-die hot, warm, and cold forging

Impression-die forging provides three-dimensional die control and is the dominant commercial forging family. The workpiece flows into matched cavities; conventional versions generate flash that is trimmed, while flashless versions tightly control billet volume so that nearly no material escapes.

The FIA guide gives the following broad steel comparison:

- cold forging: highest deformation pressure, low process energy, closest tolerances, high tooling cost;
- warm forging: intermediate force, energy, tolerance, and tooling position;
- hot forging: lowest deformation pressure and tooling cost, highest process energy, and more generous tolerances.

Fink gives a rotor-shaft temperature taxonomy of cold at 20–40°C, warm at 700–950°C, hot at or above 1,200°C, and rotary swaging as a cold/warm combination [Hirschvogel rotor-shaft paper](https://www.hirschvogel.com/fileadmin/user_upload/ATZlive_Paper_HIVO_Rotorshaft_klf_V6.pdf). Exact temperature windows depend on alloy, strain rate, lubrication, tool material, and process design.

Hot forging is forgiving of difficult geometry and high-strength steels, but creates scale, thermal gradients, larger machining allowances, and heat-treatment or straightening work. Cold forging gives better dimensional precision and surface finish, no scale, and work hardening, but requires high force and high-formability stock. Warm forging occupies the useful middle: it lowers flow stress and work hardening relative to cold forging while retaining closer tolerances than hot forging.

For hollow shafts, impression forging can form:

- an initial cup or hollow blank;
- enlarged gear or flange ends;
- stepped external contours;
- some through or blind holes;
- selected splines and axial features;
- near-net bearing or assembly regions.

Deep internal holes, undercuts, very thin walls, and complex stepped bores often remain difficult. FIA design guidance specifically warns that deep blind holes are difficult, side-wall thickness should be uniform, and extremely thin or thick tubular sections should be avoided in cold forging.

#### Flashless, near-net, and net-shape forging

Near-net forging reduces machining allowance on most surfaces. Net-shape forging can leave one or more functional surfaces without machining. The FIA guide reports that net-shape gear teeth up to 125 mm diameter have been forged to approximately ±0.10 mm in some applications, although the hole and back face still require finish machining [Forging Industry Association guide](https://www.forging.org/Common/Uploaded%20files/Design%20Engineering%20Center/Product%20Design%20Guide%20for%20Forging.pdf).

For motor shafts, the practical interpretation is selective near-net forming rather than a completely finished part. The bearing seats, spline flanks, gear teeth, datum surfaces, and bore may still require turning, broaching, grinding, honing, or hard finishing. Fink states explicitly that every forged rotor shaft in the described production context is followed by turning and drilling, with heat treatment then establishing the final hardness of splines, gears, bearings, or the shaft [Hirschvogel rotor-shaft paper](https://www.hirschvogel.com/fileadmin/user_upload/ATZlive_Paper_HIVO_Rotorshaft_klf_V6.pdf).

Near-net forging becomes more attractive as annual production increases because higher die and process costs are amortized while machining cost and material removal fall. It is less attractive when shaft variants change frequently or when the bore and gear geometry cannot be held reliably through forming and heat treatment.

### 3.2 Upsetting, heading, and end forming

Upsetting gathers material locally to enlarge an end, create a flange, form a bearing boss, or prepare a feature for subsequent forging. High-speed end forming combined with upsetting is identified by GFU as a technically plausible process combination for EV rotor shafts [GFU Forming Solutions](https://gfu-forming.de/en/rotor-shafts-for-electric-vehicles/).

Upsetting is well suited to shaft-like parts with local end features, particularly when the shaft body can remain tubular or cylindrical. It can reduce material waste compared with machining a flange from a large bar and can integrate several components into a one-piece forging.

The principal geometric limitation is unsupported length. FIA guidance states that unsupported stock gathered in one upset blow is generally limited to about three times the bar diameter unless the upset ratio and die support are controlled by additional rules. Large diameter changes may therefore require several operations. Buckling, laps, incomplete fill, and eccentricity are the main risks.

In a hollow motor-shaft route, upsetting is normally a hybrid operation rather than the complete solution:

- tube or forged blank;
- end upsetting or high-speed end forming;
- radial or impression forging of the body;
- machining and heat treatment.

### 3.3 Forward, backward, impact, and composite extrusion

Extrusion forces metal through or around a die. Forward extrusion drives material in the punch direction; backward or impact extrusion drives material opposite the punch, often around a punch to make a cup or hollow part. The FIA guide identifies forward extrusion of hollow slugs, backward extrusion of multiple inside and outside diameters, and combined extrusion sequences for shaft gears, splined shafts, and threaded shafts.

Kinefac’s spline/form extrusion is a specialized push-pull indirect process. External dies and internal mandrels move synchronously into and out of solid or hollow blanks, causing axial material flow and producing partial- or full-length internal or external forms. The supplier lists low- and medium-carbon steels, low-alloy steels, aluminum alloys, and copper alloys, with an ideal pre-extrude steel hardness of 80–100 HB and drawn-over-mandrel tubing recommended for tubular parts [Kinefac spline extrusion](https://www.kinefac.com/spline-extrusion-process/).

Kinefac claims high accuracy, repeatability, fast cycles, no material waste, comparatively high tool life, and net-shape profile production without a secondary profile-forming process. It also lists electric motor shafts among its applications. These are direct industrial application claims, but they do not specify a hollow NEV shaft’s speed, balance, bore, annual volume, tooling cost, or break-even quantity.

A 2025/2026 Chinese study proposes composite cold extrusion of a 20MnCr5 NEV transmission motor shaft using convex and concave dies with an intermediate preform. It calculates forming force and uses three-dimensional die modeling and DEFORM simulation to optimize material flow [Current Science composite extrusion study](https://currentscience.info/index.php/cs/article/view/721). This is direct NEV terminology and material evidence, but it remains theoretical and simulation-based rather than a production demonstration.

Walter Schneider’s impact-extrusion comparison assigns cold impact extrusion very low process energy, the highest precision, and suitability for simple rotationally symmetric shapes and large quantities. Hot impact extrusion is described as more suitable for complex shapes, smaller series, and harder-to-form materials, but it requires heating and has higher operating cost [Walter Schneider impact extrusion](https://www.schneider-umformen.de/en/impact-extrusion/).

A 2026 study on backward extrusion from coil demonstrates that continuous press forming can exceed 100,000 strokes using DC04 and S500MC strip on a 500 kN, 100-components-per-minute press. The tested geometry is a pin, not a hollow motor shaft, so this is evidence for a high-throughput forming platform rather than direct shaft qualification [Production Engineering coil backward extrusion](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11740-026-01433-7).

The main extrusion advantages are high repeatability, strong control of axial profiles, and potentially low material waste. The main constraints are:

- high punch and die loads;
- sensitivity to friction and lubrication;
- tool elastic deformation and wear;
- limited single-stage reduction for high-strength steels;
- need for intermediate annealing or spheroidizing;
- difficulty combining long shaft length, stepped diameter, thin wall, and deep bore in one stroke;
- possible residual stress and distortion after heat treatment.

### 3.4 Radial forging and mandrel radial forging

Radial forging reduces a workpiece incrementally with several radially oscillating dies or hammers. A mandrel controls the bore while the outside contour is simultaneously reduced or shaped. The process can be cold, warm, hot, or semi-hot.

GFM describes radial forging as using mainly four radially oscillating tools and says a mandrel can form complex internal contours in one operation. It specifically identifies EV rotor shafts as hollow and often bottle-shaped, with machining of inner diameters otherwise costly. For hybrid and pure-electric vehicles, GFM recommends semi-hot forming around 700–850°C because compact geometry and high material requirements restrict formability [GFM radial forging for automotive](https://www.gfm.at/products/radial-forging-automotive/?lang=en).

The route is attractive for a monobloc shaft because it can integrate:

- multiple stepped internal diameters;
- a single-side-closed end;
- internal spline features;
- an outer near-net contour;
- the hollow section without extensive boring;
- improved fiber flow along the shaft.

GFM reports more than 200 automotive machines and significantly more than 10 million shafts per year made by its radial forging technology. The figures establish automotive production scale, but they are not separated into EV rotor shafts [GFM radial forging for automotive](https://www.gfm.at/products/radial-forging-automotive/?lang=en).

The GFM process description claims that hollow shafts closed on one or both sides can be produced, with the inner contour near net shape and the outer contour near net shape. It also claims high forming degrees, higher fatigue strength, and economic efficiency even for smaller lots. These are supplier claims without published unit cost, cycle time, tolerance capability, or independent NEV run-at-rate data.

More direct academic evidence exists for automotive hollow stepped gear shafts. Li et al. used coupled thermo-mechanical finite-element analysis and an orthogonal design to identify 780°C initial temperature, 21° per stroke rotation, and 3 mm radial reduction as a candidate parameter combination for a hollow stepped gear shaft [Li et al., 2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11771-020-4398-7). The study found that effective strain was greatest in the outer zones and lowest in the innermost zones, indicating that through-wall strain uniformity needs process control.

TRR188 transferred an incremental radial-forging, spline-extrusion, and heat-treatment chain to industrial monobloc tubular-shaft manufacture at GKN Automotive, with numerical support from Hexagon. This is strong evidence that radial forging can be integrated into an automotive hollow-shaft chain, but the source does not report NEV-specific volume, cost, or balance performance [TRR188 industrial transfer](https://trr188.de/index.php/en/research-results/t-transfer/t04-controlling-damage-in-the-production-of-hollow-tubular-shafts-using-radial-forging-spline-extrusion-and-martensitic-hardening).

The same TRR188 work uses 34MnB5 seamless hollow material and shows that process parameters affect damage. Higher radial-feed velocity lowered calculated density, indicating increased void volume and damage; axial surface cracks were observed. Subsequent austenitizing, quenching, tempering, and coating increased strength and wear resistance, but metallography found MnO inclusions, local ferritic regions, high-aspect-ratio voids, and decarburized or damaged surface zones requiring further investigation.

A 2025 study on cold radial forging of a 20CrMnTiH hollow shaft combines spheroidizing annealing, CALPHAD, finite elements, and experiments. It reports that alloy composition and heat-treatment parameters significantly affect hardness, residual stress, effective strain, damage, and molding quality [Xu et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-025-15880-6). The route is technically credible for case-hardening steel, but no production economics or high-volume data are given.

Radial forging is consequently one of the strongest candidates for complex monobloc NEV hollow shafts, but it is not automatically the cheapest route. It requires:

- accurate mandrel and die alignment;
- control of feed, rotation, reduction, temperature, and friction;
- inspection for internal damage and surface cracks;
- machining or forming of splines and gear features;
- heat-treatment distortion validation;
- run-at-rate proof for the specific shaft.

### 3.5 Rotary swaging

Rotary swaging uses oscillating dies to reduce or shape a workpiece incrementally. Depending on the machine and tooling, it can form solid or hollow material, reduce outer diameter, control local wall thickness, and create stepped or tapered sections. It is particularly attractive when a tube is already available and the aim is to form the outside contour without extensive chip removal.

Tian et al. describe rotary swaging as capable of shaping both external and internal surfaces, locally increasing wall thickness, and achieving tolerances up to IT8 or IT9. Such capability can shorten finishing, although the result was not demonstrated on a finished hollow motor shaft [Tian et al., 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/1996-1944/17/11/2525).

Their experiment processed a solid 42CrMo rod from 25 mm to 15 mm in ten passes without additional heat treatment. It is therefore evidence of material response and preform strengthening, not direct evidence of a hollow rotor-shaft production cycle.

The measured material effects were substantial:

- tensile yield strength increased from 749 MPa to 873 MPa;
- ultimate tensile strength increased from approximately 977 MPa to 1,295 MPa;
- elongation decreased from 0.127 to 0.087;
- torsional yield strength increased from 525 MPa to 752 MPa;
- ultimate torsional strength increased from 859 MPa to 1,025 MPa.

At approximately 90 Hz and stress amplitudes of 420–480 MPa, the reported average fatigue-life increase was 45.2% at 420 MPa and 409.4% at 480 MPa. These results are useful evidence that rotary swaging can strengthen torsion-dominated steel parts, but specimen geometry and stress levels are not an NEV duty cycle.

The mechanism is not uniformly beneficial. Rotary swaging creates layered strain hardening and residual stress. Tian et al. found that fatigue cracks in the tested rods shifted from predominantly surface-controlled behavior toward a combination of internal and surface crack initiation. Ductility fell, and the authors caution that the process response depends on strain distribution, residual stress, texture, and deformation history.

For hollow tubes, friction is a central control variable. A 2021 numerical study found final wall-thickness differences up to 8.2% in one thin tube case and 2.8% in a thicker case, concluding that thinner tubes are more sensitive to friction fluctuations [Liu et al., 2021](https://www.mdpi.com/1996-1944/14/1/58). This is directly relevant to a 4–6 mm-wall rotor shaft: lubricant condition, die wear, tube ovality, and pass schedule must be controlled statistically.

Felss presents a rotor-shaft chain using a tubular product, rotary swaging, and axial forming across six mainly cold-forming stations. The process distributes wall thickness according to load, integrates helical gearing, and avoids heating. Felss reports a Generation E10 six-jaw unit with up to 6,000 kN forming force and forming frequency up to 50 Hz [Felss rotor-shaft process chain](https://felss.com/en/blog/from-cost-factor-to-competitive-advantage-an-efficient-process-chain-for-rotor-shafts/). Its FRED analysis reports more than 60% lower CO₂ emissions, approximately 4 kg CO₂ saved per rotor shaft, against a machining reference at an assumed 200,000 components per year. This is an emissions comparison, not a direct unit-cost or qualification result.

Rotary swaging is therefore a leading tube-based candidate where:

- a seamless or drawn tube is available;
- the shaft has a mostly tubular profile;
- variable wall thickness is useful;
- integrated helical or axial features are valuable;
- the material can withstand incremental cold or warm deformation;
- wall-thickness and residual-stress capability can be demonstrated.

### 3.6 Axial forming, spline extrusion, and spline rolling

These processes usually form a feature rather than the whole shaft.

Fink identifies broaching and axial forming as state-of-the-art internal-spline processes. Axial forming is preferred when the internal geometry does not leave enough space for a broaching tool, but it requires approximately 2–3 mm of spline-end run-out space. The source reports ISO 1328 spline tolerance values of 7–8 for axial forming and 8–9 for outer-spline rolling [Hirschvogel rotor-shaft paper](https://www.hirschvogel.com/fileadmin/user_upload/ATZlive_Paper_HIVO_Rotorshaft_klf_V6.pdf).

Profiroll’s Thruforce route clamps a hollow workpiece between centers and synchronizes two shaped dies while the workpiece moves axially. The process forms a full-length involute spline on a thin-walled hollow rotor shaft. The supplier warns that excessive tension can widen or deform the tube, worsen runout, and increase total pitch error; mandrel-free operation and cost reduction are therefore conditional on precise process control [Profiroll hollow rotor shaft](https://www.profiroll.com/fileadmin/user_upload/4_verfahren/5_Bibliothek/eMobility-Rotor_shaft.pdf).

Kinefac’s push-pull spline/form extrusion can produce partial- or full-length profiles on hollow blanks and claims net-shape production. It is attractive for high-volume, repeatable axial features, but the form-tool accuracy controls the result and the process does not eliminate all shaft machining.

These processes are most suitable as part of a hybrid route:

- form the hollow body by forging, swaging, extrusion, or tube forming;
- form the internal or external spline before hardening;
- heat treat the spline and shaft;
- hard turn, grind, or hone the bearing and gear surfaces;
- dynamically balance the rotor.

### 3.7 Cross-wedge rolling, skew rolling, and multi-wedge rolling

Cross-wedge rolling (CWR), also called skew rolling in some configurations, uses wedge-shaped tools or rolls to reduce and redistribute material incrementally. Knifing, stretching, and sizing zones shape rotationally symmetric workpieces. It can use solid or hollow billets, mandrels, or combined operations.

The process has strong material and equipment arguments. A 2023 Metals study compared mandrel CWR with hot extrusion for an axle sleeve at 1,100°C. Maximum CWR force was about 100 kN versus 3,084 kN for hot extrusion, and the authors reported approximately 10% higher material utilization and 15% lower energy consumption for the combined route [Metals CWR study](https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4701/13/6/1017). These values apply to an axle sleeve, not an NEV shaft.

The same study reported well-formed inner holes and improved eccentricity in the deformed region: a maximum wall-thickness difference fell from 1.5 mm in the initial eccentric billet to 0.3 mm after rolling. Again, the result is geometry-specific.

Direct motor-shaft evidence is older and more limited. A 2013 study established a Deform-3D model of hollow motor-shaft forming using four-roll CWR and reported simulated maximum rolling force up to 60 kN [Applied Mechanics and Materials study](https://doi.org/10.4028/www.scientific.net/amm.288.267). It did not provide production tolerance, cost, balance, or fatigue results.

A 2022 three-roller skew-rolling study modeled a 51 mm diameter, 8 mm wall, 320 mm long S355 tube and compared it with a solid bar. The hollow case required lower modeled loads—26 kN tool load, 13.5 kN chuck load, and below 270 Nm torque—than the solid case, which reached 33 kN, 18.5 kN, and approximately 720 Nm [AJSE skew-rolling study](https://doi.org/10.1007/s43452-021-00205-7). The hollow billet flowed radially toward the axis, increasing wall thickness and producing little elongation, while the solid billet elongated substantially.

The study also reports a lower predicted Cockcroft–Latham ductile-fracture criterion for three-tool rolling than for two-tool rolling. It interprets this as a lower internal-cracking probability, but the values are model outputs rather than direct crack-rate measurements.

CWR has several limitations:

- central Mannesmann cavities and internal cracks can form;
- surface hollows caused by roll damage may be uncorrectable by finishing;
- the outer profile may require machining allowance;
- tool wear can be severe;
- hollow-billet wall flow depends on mandrel size, wall thickness, wedge geometry, temperature, and friction;
- industrial adoption is less established for NEV rotor shafts than for general shaft preforms.

A 2023 pinion-shaft study found near-net CWR geometry but still required positive machining allowance. It also observed central Mannesmann cavities in some 20MnCr5/higher-alloy combinations, first tool-wear signs after five experiments, and a tool too worn for further tests after 30 experiments. Joining interfaces failed at 1,100–1,200°C in some hybrid materials [Merkel et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12289-023-01761-4). CWR should therefore be treated as a conditional preform route rather than a universal replacement for forging.

### 3.8 Rotary compression and rotary forging

Rotary compression uses tools that rotate and translate relative to the workpiece axis. The tool contact area is smaller than in a conventional press, which can reduce force and form stepped hollow shafts over a mandrel.

Pater and colleagues used three-dimensional finite-element modeling and laboratory experiments to confirm production of stepped hollow axes and shafts by rotary compression [Pater et al.](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1016/j.acme.2014.10.002). Related work found that tubular billet wall thickness affects metal-flow kinematics and final shaft geometry [Tomczak, Bulzak & Pater](https://doi.org/10.5545/sv-jme.2014.1977).

The route is technically credible for prototypes and specialized preforms, especially when:

- several diameters must be formed along the length;
- a mandrel can control the bore;
- tooling flexibility is more important than maximum throughput;
- the shaft is too complex for a single extrusion stroke.

However, the supplied evidence is laboratory-based. It does not establish production OEE, tool life, unit cost, balance, spline quality, or high-volume NEV qualification.

General rotary forging guidance claims 5–20% lower force than conventional forming because of reduced contact and friction, but this is not hollow-motor-shaft-specific evidence [Total Materia rotary forging](https://www.totalmateria.com/en-us/articles/rotary-forging/).

### 3.9 Ring rolling

Ring rolling starts from an upset and pierced donut-shaped preform. A drive roll and mandrel reduce wall thickness and increase diameter, while axial rolls may control ring height. The process produces seamless rings with good material utilization and forged properties. The FIA guide reports that the preform can use up to 95% of the starting billet and that ring sections often require little or no machining [Forging Industry Association guide](https://www.forging.org/Common/Uploaded%20files/Design%20Engineering%20Center/Product%20Design%20Guide%20for%20Forging.pdf).

Ring rolling is not normally a complete process for a long NEV rotor shaft. It is relevant when the shaft design includes:

- an annular flange;
- a rotor ring or separate ring component;
- a short hollow section;
- a ring preform later joined or forged into the shaft.

For a conventional 200–350 mm long motor shaft, ring rolling would usually be a component or preform operation, not the primary complete-shaft route.

### 3.10 Seamless tube manufacture, drawing, and sinking

A seamless tube route begins with a solid billet. Mannesmann piercing creates a central hole, a mandrel mill elongates the hollow shell while reducing wall thickness, and a stretch reducer sizes the outside diameter. Cold drawing, cold sinking, end thickening, and internal grinding can then produce a tube with tighter dimensions.

A patent for automotive seamless drive-shaft tubes describes this sequence and identifies the importance of internal-surface quality. Without an inner tool, stretch reduction can create longitudinal wrinkles and polygonal inner surfaces. Repeated cold drawing and intermediate annealing can improve smoothness but raise cost [seamless steel tube patent](https://www.freepatentsonline.com/y2005/0266927.html).

The same source describes 15–25 mm inside diameters and reports that removing 20–500 μm from the inner surface by shot blasting could take several tens of minutes to several hours in a conventional route. Its proposed process uses reheating at 800–1,050°C, sizing, inside grinding with approximately 10 minutes for 20–30 μm removal, and cold drawing or rolling to reach Ra 1–4 μm. These are patent examples for automotive drive-shaft tubes, not validated motor-shaft production figures.

Seamless tube manufacture is attractive when the shaft is fundamentally a long tube with relatively simple external geometry. It is less attractive when the shaft needs:

- thickened bearing ends;
- integrated gears;
- sharply stepped internal contours;
- internal splines;
- a one-piece closed-end geometry;
- very high concentricity after heat treatment.

A practical hybrid route can use seamless tube as a starting blank, then apply rotary swaging, end upsetting, radial forging, axial spline forming, or friction welding.

### 3.11 Flow forming, tube spinning, and rotary drawing

Flow forming uses one or more rollers to reduce wall thickness and extend or shape a tube over a mandrel. Tube spinning and shear forming use localized roller contact to generate cylindrical, conical, or stepped shapes. Rotary drawing can form a thick-walled tube or sheet workpiece over a mandrel.

A 2024 tube-spinning review identifies simple tooling and good surface finish as key advantages, while warning that large plastic deformation changes microstructure and mechanical properties [Tube spinning review](https://www.sciopen.com/article/10.51393/j.jamst.2024014). A review of heat-assisted spinning reports improved formability and reduced force in high-strength steels, aluminum, titanium, and magnesium alloys, but also emphasizes temperature-control and multi-pass effects [Heat-Assisted Metal Spinning review](https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4701/16/5/483).

The review identifies furnace, flame, hot-gas, induction, laser, and heated-tool heating variants. It reports that moderate thinning of 10–20% per pass often balances recrystallization and work hardening in hot spinning and flow forming, while intermediate annealing or controlled cooling can reduce residual stress but may introduce distortion.

Nagimov et al. studied hot rotary drawing of thick-walled workpieces for thin-walled gas-turbine shafts. Computer and physical modeling were used to determine the initial workpiece and mandrel geometry, and full-size EI962-Sh chromium-steel shafts were rolled [Nagimov et al., 2017](https://doi.org/10.3103/s1052618817060103). This establishes technical process precedent, but not NEV motor-shaft production.

Flow forming and spinning are therefore promising for:

- thin-wall tubular shafts;
- low-to-medium volume or variant-rich products;
- prototype and pilot development;
- aluminum or difficult-to-form alloys when hot assistance is available;
- preforms later finished by swaging or radial forging.

Their limitations are pass count, wall-thickness uniformity, residual stress, mandrel and roller wear, thermal control, and the lack of direct high-volume NEV shaft data.

### 3.12 Tube hydroforming and hot metal gas forming

Tube hydroforming uses internal hydraulic pressure, often combined with axial feeding, to press a tube against a die and create a stepped or contoured external profile. A 2024 review classifies tube hydroforming and sheet hydroforming separately and identifies automotive frames, exhaust systems, and structural components as established applications [hydroforming review](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s44147-024-00546-z).

Hydroforming can produce uniform wall distribution, low assembly count, and complex external contours. The review reports claims of lower workpiece and tooling costs and lower weight compared with welding and stamping, but also identifies high tooling cost, high capital intensity, complex process control, limited material selection, maintenance, and longer cycles than traditional forming. It favors ductile steels and aluminum over harder materials.

The review gives broad pressure ranges:

- low-pressure hydroforming: 1,000–10,000 psi, approximately 70–700 bar;
- high-pressure hydroforming: 20,000–70,000 psi, approximately 1,400–4,800 bar.

Pressure, axial feed, friction, strain-hardening behavior, temperature, and loading path determine whether the tube wrinkles, necks, cracks, or fills the die. Warm hydroforming can extend the process to ultrahigh-strength steel, 6xxx and 7xxx aluminum, and steel–aluminum hybrids. Hot metal gas forming can improve formability and dimensional accuracy in tubular profiles, but the review still identifies material-model and microstructural research needs.

Hydroforming is a plausible NEV shaft-preform route where:

- the shaft is tube-compatible;
- external complexity dominates;
- annual volume is high enough to amortize dedicated dies and high-pressure equipment;
- the material is ductile enough;
- final bearing, spline, gear, and balance operations remain acceptable.

The available evidence does not establish hydroforming as a production route for a high-speed traction-motor shaft. It should be evaluated as a hybrid preform process, not selected solely because it is attractive for automotive structural tubes.

### 3.13 Friction-welded, nested-tube, and split-structure shafts

A hollow shaft may be assembled from two tubes, a tube and forged ends, or separate rotor and flange parts. Friction welding is attractive because it avoids filler metal and can produce a consolidated joint with limited heat input.

The patent US20160305469A1 describes swaging one tube until its outside diameter fits inside another, nesting the tubes, optionally applying torsion in different directions, and friction-welding the stems. The claimed purpose is improved bidirectional durability under regenerative-braking-type torque reversals. The patent does not report motor-shaft balance, weld fatigue, runout, cycle time, or unit cost.

Profiroll describes an assembled hollow rotor shaft in which a rotor and two flange parts are manufactured separately and welded. The flanges include bearing seats and output-gear connections; the report emphasizes that runout among the components must be very good [Profiroll hollow rotor shaft](https://www.profiroll.com/fileadmin/user_upload/4_verfahren/5_Bibliothek/eMobility-Rotor_shaft.pdf).

The 2025 T/CAAMTB specification specifically covers hollow split-structure motor shafts press-fitted at room temperature and also applies to NEV generator shafts [T/CAAMTB 265-2025](https://ndls.cnis.ac.cn/standard/detail/e69a321a53a870b0b33c0d0ad403f82b). This is evidence that split architecture is a recognized NEV manufacturing option, but not evidence that it is superior to a monobloc forged shaft.

Split or welded construction can reduce forming complexity and permit different materials or locally optimized features. It adds:

- weld or press-fit fatigue risk;
- joint concentricity and runout control;
- balance correction;
- weld integrity inspection;
- thermal distortion;
- additional assembly and traceability;
- possible corrosion or interface issues.

It is best considered when a monobloc hollow shaft cannot economically form the end features, or when the architecture deliberately separates a thin tubular torque body from forged bearing or gear ends.

### 3.14 Powder forging and additive manufacture

Powder forging can produce dense, near-net, axisymmetric components at high volume. The FIA guide identifies it as an alternative to impression-die forging for small and medium, highly symmetric automotive components such as gears and connecting rods. However, the supplied evidence does not show a hollow NEV rotor shaft made by powder forging. Hollow compaction, density gradients, bore quality, fatigue, and cost would all require specific qualification.

Additive manufacture can create internal passages, lattices, and geometry that is difficult to form conventionally. EOS lists 20MnCr5 and 42CrMo4 powders for automotive and general-engineering parts, shafts, and gears. It reports heat-treatable material capability and typical tensile properties for its powder systems [EOS steel powders](https://www.eos.info/metal-solutions/metal-materials/other-steels).

That evidence establishes material availability, not production qualification. For a high-speed hollow rotor shaft, additive manufacturing would still require proof of:

- density and internal defect control;
- anisotropic fatigue properties;
- surface integrity and bore finishing;
- residual-stress relief;
- dimensional stability after heat treatment;
- balance and critical-speed behavior;
- build rate and cost;
- repeatability across machines and powder lots.

On the available evidence, additive manufacture is suitable for prototypes, tooling, special low-volume shafts, or development of internal cooling concepts—not as a qualified high-volume default.

## 4. Material compatibility and heat-treatment selection

### 4.1 Steel grades

Steel remains the default because it combines high torsional strength, stiffness, fatigue resistance, established heat treatment, and a mature automotive supply base.

| Material family | Useful forming routes | Typical heat treatment | Main advantage | Main caution |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20MnCr5 / 20CrMnTi | Cold or warm forging, extrusion, radial forging, CWR, tube-based routes | Carburizing or carbonitriding, quench and temper | Hard wear-resistant surface with tough core | Carburizing cost and distortion; weldability is poor |
| 20CrNiMo / 18CrNiMo7-6 | Hot/warm forging, radial forging, extrusion, machining | Carburizing or carbonitriding | High hardenability and fatigue-oriented case/core combination | More alloy and heat-treatment cost; route-specific data limited |
| 40Cr / 40CrH | Hot, warm, cold with suitable condition; radial forging; machining | Quench and temper, optional induction | Low-cost, readily available, straightforward treatment | Lower hardenability and fatigue margin than 42CrMo in demanding sections |
| 42CrMo4 / 4140 | Warm or hot forging, radial forging, rotary swaging, extrusion, machining | Quench and temper, local induction hardening | Strength, toughness, hardenability, broad industrial use | Higher flow stress and moderate machinability; distortion must be controlled |
| 4340 | Hot/warm forging, machining, selected cold or warm forming after conditioning | Quench and temper or induction | Higher toughness and high-cycle capability | Premium material and processing cost |
| 34MnB5 | Radial forging, tube and automotive hollow-shaft routes | Quench, temper, coating or related martensitic treatment | Automotive hollow-shaft precedent | Damage, voids, inclusions, and decarburization require control |
| S355, 45#, carbon steels | CWR, skew rolling, general forging | Route-specific | Good formability and low material cost | Usually an analogue or preform material, not the default high-speed shaft grade |

The T/ZJDJ 002-2022 specification provides a useful NEV-specific treatment split. For 20CrMnTi, 20CrNiMo, and related low-carbon grades, it specifies carburizing or carbonitriding with surface hardness HRC58–63, core hardness HRC30–45, and an effective hardened layer generally in the 0.3–1.3 mm range, adjustable to strength and torque. For 40Cr and 42CrMo, it specifies quench-and-temper treatment before precision machining followed by induction hardening to HRC50–58 with an effective hardened layer of 0.5–5 mm, again adjustable to the application [T/ZJDJ 002-2022](https://ndls.cnis.ac.cn/standard/detail/1bf70fee23d908c4df27c754520158da).

Fink identifies 42CrMo4 and 20MnCr5 as common rotor-shaft choices because a hard surface can provide wear resistance while the core remains tough. JEC’s supplier dataset identifies 4140/42CrMo4 with induction hardening as its standard EV traction-motor shaft material and 4340 as a premium option for sustained peak torque above 600 Nm and high cycle counts [Hirschvogel rotor-shaft paper](https://www.hirschvogel.com/fileadmin/user_upload/ATZlive_Paper_HIVO_Rotorshaft_klf_V6.pdf); [JEC EV shaft requirements](https://www.motor-shaft.com/news/ev-motor-shaft-requirements-high-speed-high-torque-and-lightweight-design-challenges/).

These recommendations are not identical because the dominant failure mode differs:

- carburized 20MnCr5 or 20CrMnTi is attractive where spline or gear flank wear and contact fatigue dominate;
- induction-hardened 42CrMo4 is attractive where a strong, tough shaft body and localized hard surfaces are needed;
- 4340 or 18CrNiMo7-6 becomes more attractive when sustained high torque, impact, or high cycle count justifies the premium;
- 40Cr is suitable only when the shaft diameter and duty allow its lower strength and hardenability margin.

The International Molybdenum Association describes carburized steels as combining a hard, wear-resistant case with a tough, impact-resistant core. It lists 20MnCr5 and 18CrNiMo7-6 compositions but does not rank them for hollow motor-shaft cost or formability [IMOA case-hardening steels](https://www.imoa.info/molybdenum-uses/molybdenum-grade-alloy-steels-irons/case-hardening-steel.php).

### 4.2 Aluminum and other light alloys

Aluminum is attractive for weight reduction and corrosion resistance, and the FIA guide identifies aluminum as readily forgeable into precise shapes. It lists 6061-T6 and 7075-T6 among common forging alloys and gives an approximate general service-temperature limit of 150°C for aluminum forgings [Forging Industry Association guide](https://www.forging.org/Common/Uploaded%20files/Design%20Engineering%20Center/Product%20Design%20Guide%20for%20Forging.pdf).

Applicable processes include:

- hot impression forging;
- tube extrusion;
- tube drawing;
- hydroforming;
- flow forming and spinning;
- rotary swaging;
- cross-wedge rolling;
- friction-welded hybrid construction.

The supplied evidence contains several material-specific examples:

- a CWR study used an aluminum-alloy hollow shaft and modeled grain-size changes with temperature and reduction [Yu et al.](https://journal.hep.com.cn/jocsu/EN/10.1007/s11771-022-4950-8);
- a CWR pinion study used EN-AW 6082 joined to 20MnCr5 and reported 33% component-weight reduction, but required matched forming conditions for dissimilar yield stresses [Merkel et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12289-023-01761-4);
- rotary-swaging literature includes aluminum wire and 1050 aluminum, with fatigue-limit gains but also reduced ductility and increased fatigue-crack growth in some conditions [Tian et al., 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/1996-1944/17/11/2525);
- the hydroforming review discusses 6xxx and 7xxx aluminum in warm hydroforming.

None of these results establishes a steel-equivalent aluminum hollow rotor shaft at 15,000–22,000 rpm, with the required bearing fits, spline hardness, thermal stability, and fatigue margin. Aluminum also has lower elastic modulus than steel, so equal outside diameter does not mean equal bending stiffness. It may be viable for a specific low-load or hybrid shaft, but it requires system-level rotor-dynamics and fatigue validation.

Magnesium offers lower density but lower modulus, lower strength at elevated temperature, corrosion sensitivity, and more difficult handling. Titanium offers high specific strength but expensive material, difficult forming, tool wear, contamination control, and high cost. Copper is highly conductive but generally unsuitable as the primary torque-carrying shaft body. Stainless steels can provide corrosion or temperature resistance but require higher forming forces and may be more expensive.

Nickel alloys and other high-temperature alloys are technically forgeable, but their service advantages are not normally needed in a passenger-vehicle traction shaft and their forming and material costs are unfavorable. The available evidence should therefore be interpreted as route compatibility, not as a recommendation for these materials.

### 4.3 Material condition and formability

Material condition can determine whether a nominally compatible process is practical:

- cold forging favors low-to-medium carbon, low-alloy, relatively soft stock with adequate elongation and reduction of area;
- warm forging expands the process window for higher-alloy steels and larger reductions;
- hot forging accommodates high strength and complex geometry but adds scale and thermal variation;
- rotary swaging can cold-work 42CrMo, but the resulting strength increase is accompanied by reduced ductility and layered residual stress;
- radial forging can use semi-hot material and a mandrel to control complex contours;
- tube processes require controlled tube ovality, wall variation, and surface quality before forming;
- carburizing and induction hardening change dimensions and can introduce shaft bending;
- aluminum and titanium require temperature and strain-rate control;
- dissimilar material joining adds interface-specific formability and fatigue risk.

A 2025 20CrMnTiH cold-radial-forging study found that alloy chemistry and spheroidizing-annealing conditions affect hardness, residual stress, effective strain, and damage [Xu et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-025-15880-6). This supports a process-specific material window rather than a simple list of grades.

## 5. Economics, scalability, and downstream processing

### 5.1 What “cost-effective” means for this part

For a hollow motor shaft, unit cost is not the forming-machine price alone. A useful comparison is:

\[
C_{\mathrm{good\ shaft}}=\frac{C_{\mathrm{material}}+C_{\mathrm{tooling}}+C_{\mathrm{capital}}+C_{\mathrm{labor}}+C_{\mathrm{energy}}+C_{\mathrm{scrap}}+C_{\mathrm{downstream}}+C_{\mathrm{quality}}}{N_{\mathrm{good\ shafts}}}
\]

This is a decision model, not a supplied industry calculation. The denominator must be good shafts, not gross strokes, because scrap, rework, heat-treatment distortion, balancing failures, and inspection rejects can dominate the apparent forming cost.

The relevant cost drivers are:

- raw material price and purchase form;
- material yield and engineered scrap;
- die, mandrel, roller, punch, and fixture cost;
- press, radial-forging, swaging, hydroforming, or spinning capital;
- heating and atmosphere cost;
- tool life and maintenance;
- forming cycle time and number of passes;
- automation and handling;
- machining allowance and chip volume;
- heat treatment, straightening, grinding, and balancing;
- inspection and traceability;
- volume stability over the product life.

The [FIA forging guide](https://www.forging.org/Common/Uploaded%20files/Design%20Engineering%20Center/Product%20Design%20Guide%20for%20Forging.pdf) states that actual forging cost must be obtained from the producer and that higher precision trades higher forming and tooling cost against lower machining cost. It also notes that cold-forging tooling, including typical automation, can cost five to ten times as much as equivalent hot impression-die tooling, although cold-forging tool life is generally longer.

### 5.2 Volume sensitivity and break-even evidence

The evidence supports a directional rather than numerical volume ranking.

#### Low volume and frequent variants

Machining from tube or bar, open-die or mandrel forging, rotary compression, spinning, and flexible radial forging minimize dedicated tooling exposure. They have higher piece cost, but the investment is easier to justify when:

- annual shaft volume is uncertain;
- several shaft variants share a platform;
- geometry is still changing;
- the program requires rapid prototypes;
- tooling amortization would dominate.

The FIA guide says open-die forging has little chargeable tooling cost and short lead time but higher per-piece cost, lower precision, and more machining than impression-die forging.

#### Serial production

Warm forging, radial forging, rotary swaging, tube drawing, CWR, and integrated machining become competitive when a stable shaft family can share tooling and fixtures. The best route depends on whether the main saving comes from:

- reduced raw-material diameter;
- reduced boring;
- reduced external turning;
- integrated spline or gear forming;
- shorter heat-treatment chain;
- lower balancing and rework rates.

#### High volume

Cold forging, flashless or near-net impression forging, spline extrusion, automated rotary swaging, dedicated tube forming, and integrated machining lines become attractive when the design is stable and the annual quantity is high enough to amortize tooling.

FIA’s general guide associates impression-die forging with 300 or more pieces typically and cold forging with usually more than 10,000, but neither value is a shaft-specific break-even. Zhang et al.’s cost model for a 20CrMnTi hollow gear shaft found that the route called “Cold Extrusion 2” became the lowest modeled cost at 90 mm shaft length despite having the highest material cost because its rough-processing and wasted-material costs were lowest. The model was fixed-volume, design-specific, and excluded differentiation of fine finishing [Zhang et al., 2018](https://publica.fraunhofer.de/bitstreams/a343908c-8dd5-4ed6-bcbf-366b0a2a9d09/download).

DVS reports that an integrated machine combining turning, milling, drilling, and gear skiving can soft-machine hollow shafts in two setups and is designed for approximately 50,000–100,000 pieces per year. It reports up to 40% lower cost than conventional production in some cases, but this is an integrated machining-chain claim, not a forming-route comparison [DVS e-shaft production](https://blog.dvs-technology.com/en/posts/with-an-integrated-production-solution-for-the-perfect-e-shaft).

No defensible statement can therefore be made that, for example, radial forging becomes cheaper than swaging at a particular annual volume. The strongest supported conclusion is that dedicated cold, warm, radial, extrusion, or integrated tube-forming routes should be considered when quantity, design stability, and the avoided machining burden justify the tooling and qualification work.

### 5.3 Material utilization and energy

Forming normally reduces chip volume compared with machining from bar. Fink identifies poor material utilization as a disadvantage of unformed machined parts because of high chip volume [Hirschvogel rotor-shaft paper](https://www.hirschvogel.com/fileadmin/user_upload/ATZlive_Paper_HIVO_Rotorshaft_klf_V6.pdf).

Route-specific evidence is directional:

- ring rolling can use up to 95% of the starting billet in the preform;
- CWR plus extrusion produced approximately 10% higher material utilization and 15% lower energy consumption than the compared axle-sleeve route;
- Felss reports six mainly cold-forming stations with no heating and more than 60% lower CO₂ emissions than a machining reference in its scenario;
- cold extrusion avoids process heat but requires high forming force;
- hot forging lowers forming force but consumes heating energy and produces scale;
- hydroforming can save material compared with welded/stamped structures but requires high-pressure equipment and complex control;
- extensive tube inside grinding can eliminate the material-utilization advantage of a seamless tube.

These figures are not directly comparable because they use different reference routes, geometries, system boundaries, and production assumptions.

### 5.4 Common downstream process chain

A formed hollow shaft normally follows a sequence such as:

1. **Blank preparation.** Sawing, tube cutting, billet conditioning, end facing, cleaning, or preliminary annealing/spheroidizing.
2. **Primary hollow forming.** Forging, extrusion, swaging, radial forging, rolling, hydroforming, spinning, or a combination.
3. **Reference and rough machining.** Turning of outside diameters, end faces, bearing envelopes, and internal bores; drilling or boring where the bore is not already at the required size.
4. **Torque-feature forming.** Broaching, axial forming, spline extrusion, spline rolling, gear milling, or helical-gear forming.
5. **Heat treatment.** Carburizing or carbonitriding for low-carbon case-hardening steels; quench and temper for 40Cr or 42CrMo; induction hardening of journals, splines, or seal surfaces; solution treatment and aging for aluminum where applicable.
6. **Distortion correction.** Straightening, sizing, coining, or controlled correction after heat treatment.
7. **Hard finishing.** Hard turning, cylindrical grinding, internal grinding, honing, gear grinding, or gear honing.
8. **Balancing and cleaning.** Dynamic balance correction, demagnetization where required, bore cleaning, washing, drying, and particulate verification.
9. **Inspection and traceability.** Dimensional measurement, CMM, runout, wall thickness, hardness, case depth, NDT, surface finish, marking, and final functional or rotor testing.

Fink’s implemented sample flow is concrete: cold forging, right and left turning, data-matrix milling, oil-cooling-hole drilling, axial inner-spline forming, induction hardening, hard turning, grinding, marking, demagnetization, and inspection [Hirschvogel rotor-shaft paper](https://www.hirschvogel.com/fileadmin/user_upload/ATZlive_Paper_HIVO_Rotorshaft_klf_V6.pdf).

### 5.5 Route-specific downstream burden

| Forming route | Likely machining allowance and finishing | Heat-treatment burden | Feature and inspection burden |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cold or warm near-net forging | Low to moderate external allowance; bore and precision seats normally machined | Q&T, carburizing, or induction depending grade | Strong need for die-volume control, dimensional inspection, and distortion correction |
| Semi-hot radial forging | Near-net internal and external contours claimed; bearing and datum surfaces still finished | Often Q&T, case hardening, or induction | Bore eccentricity, feed damage, mandrel wear, wall thickness, internal NDT |
| Rotary swaging | Potentially low allowance; IT8–IT9 claimed for some hollow-shaft work | Cold-work stress relief, Q&T, carburizing, or induction as required | Friction-sensitive wall thickness, residual stress, pass-to-pass traceability |
| Spline/form extrusion | Profile may be net shape; body, bore, seats, and runout still require finishing | Hardening after profile formation | Form-tool accuracy, spline pitch, flank hardness, run-out space |
| CWR/skew rolling | Positive machining allowance generally required; profile not necessarily final | Heat treatment and distortion validation | Surface hollows, Mannesmann cavity, tool wear, optical or dimensional inspection |
| Seamless tube/drawing | Inside grinding, cold drawing, end sinking, turning, and boring may be substantial | Annealing between draws and final hardening | Inner-surface wrinkles, ovality, wall variation, cleanliness |
| Hydroforming | External shape may be near net; ends and functional surfaces require machining | Material-specific treatment and distortion study | Pressure, leakage, wrinkles, axial feed, wall-thickness mapping |
| Spinning/flow forming | Multiple passes and possible intermediate anneal | Residual-stress relief and final hardening | Thickness distribution, mandrel control, ovality, thermal distortion |
| Split or welded construction | Machining after welding is needed to establish common datums | Local heat-treatment or post-weld stress effects | Weld integrity, joint runout, balance, leak or fatigue testing |
| Machining from bar/tube | No forming allowance, but very high chip volume | Treatment after rough machining | Flexible but expensive; easy to inspect during development |

FIA guidance gives approximately 1.25–2.5 mm finish allowance plus draft for typical finished hot forgings and at least 5 mm of machining envelope per 300 mm for blocker-type steel forgings. These are general guidelines; they should not be imposed on a precision rotor shaft without supplier confirmation.

For tight bearing fits, Le Creator reports turned capability around IT7–IT9 and Ra approximately 1.6 μm, compared with ground journals around IT5–IT6 and Ra 0.2–0.4 μm. It reports approximately 0.10–0.30 mm grinding stock on turned journals and IT5–IT6, Ra ≤0.2 μm for ID grinding or honing of hollow bores [Le Creator motor-shaft machining](https://le-creator.com/blog/motor-shaft-machining/). These values are process bands, not guaranteed shaft capability.

## 6. Technical performance, quality risks, and scalability

### 6.1 Dimensional accuracy and wall-thickness control

The most important distinction is between as-formed accuracy and final shaft accuracy. A forming process may produce an excellent preform while still requiring grinding to achieve the bearing, spline, and gear requirements.

- **Cold forging and extrusion** offer strong dimensional repeatability but are sensitive to tool elastic deflection, material volume, lubrication, and work hardening.
- **Warm forging** relaxes the force and formability limits but introduces thermal variation and shrinkage.
- **Hot forging and radial forging** support complex geometry but usually require more finishing and careful temperature control.
- **Rotary swaging** can achieve close tolerances, but friction can create longitudinal wall variation, especially in thin tubes.
- **CWR** can improve bore eccentricity in the deformed region, but initial billet eccentricity, mandrel design, and wedge damage remain important.
