- **Hydroforming** can provide uniform wall distribution in a suitable tube, but pressure and axial feed must be controlled to avoid wrinkles or local thinning.
- **Spinning and flow forming** provide flexible geometry but require pass-by-pass wall-thickness measurement.
- **Tube drawing and sinking** can provide accurate size and surface finish but may require repeated annealing and inside treatment.

The shaft’s final concentricity is a chain property. Bore, outside diameter, bearing seats, spline axis, gear axis, rotor-stack seat, and correction planes must share a controlled datum strategy. Fink reports 7–12 μm bearing-length OD tolerance and 5–8 μm cylindricity as high-speed rotor-shaft experience, while an IMARC e-axle facility reports ±5 μm stator and rotor concentricity at facility level and G2.5 rotor balancing. The IMARC values are not identified as hollow-shaft tolerances [Hirschvogel rotor-shaft paper](https://www.hirschvogel.com/fileadmin/user_upload/ATZlive_Paper_HIVO_Rotorshaft_klf_V6.pdf); [IMARC e-axle facility](https://www.imarcengineering.com/case-study/electric-motor-and-e-axle-manufacturing-facility).

### 6.2 Fiber flow, fatigue, and torsional strength

Forging can improve fatigue performance when the fiber flow follows the principal load path. The FIA guide explains that forging refines grain structure, produces directional grain flow, and can improve tensile, impact, fracture, and fatigue properties. Fink adds an important warning: unfavorable fiber orientation protruding perpendicularly from a surface can increase fatigue and pitting susceptibility [Forging Industry Association guide](https://www.forging.org/Common/Uploaded%20files/Design%20Engineering%20Center/Product%20Design%20Guide%20for%20Forging.pdf); [Hirschvogel rotor-shaft paper](https://www.hirschvogel.com/fileadmin/user_upload/ATZlive_Paper_HIVO_Rotorshaft_klf_V6.pdf).

Rotary swaging produces a different strengthening mechanism. Tian et al.’s 42CrMo tests show improved torsional strength and fatigue life, but the specimen developed layered strain hardening, residual stress, reduced elongation, and internal fatigue origins. A formed hollow shaft may behave differently because the bore changes the strain gradient and because the final shaft has splines, holes, bearing transitions, and heat-treated surfaces.

Radial forging can align flow around a hollow contour, but TRR188 demonstrates that excessive feed velocity can increase void volume and that damage can appear as axial cracks. CWR can reduce equipment force and improve material utilization, but central Mannesmann cavities and surface hollows can become fatigue initiators. Seamless tubes can have inner wrinkles that become fatigue-crack initiation sites after quenching [seamless steel tube patent](https://www.freepatentsonline.com/y2005/0266927.html).

A 2026 study of heat-treated 42CrMo4 EV motor shafts examined magnetorheological finishing rather than forming. It reported roughness reduction from 0.18–0.22 μm to 0.013–0.020 μm, a shift from +150 MPa tensile residual stress to −160 to −230 MPa compressive residual stress, and an approximately 39% fatigue-life improvement. The abstract does not state sample size, cycle time, production rate, or industrial-scale validation [MR finishing study](https://doi.org/10.1177/09544089261419663). This result illustrates why post-forming surface integrity can materially affect fatigue, but it should not be used to rank forming methods.

### 6.3 Defect mechanisms by route

| Route | Principal defect mechanisms | Practical controls |
|---|---|---|
| Impression forging | Laps, folds, underfill, flash variation, die mismatch, scale, grain-flow interruption | Preform design, billet-volume control, die maintenance, hot inspection, MPI and dimensional capability |
| Cold/warm extrusion | Cracking, galling, punch failure, residual stress, incomplete fill | Annealed stock, lubrication, staged reduction, tool-strength analysis, intermediate anneal |
| Radial forging | Bore eccentricity, axial cracks, void growth, surface damage, mandrel marks | Feed/rotation/reduction control, mandrel alignment, temperature monitoring, UT/MPI, metallography |
| Rotary swaging | Wall-thickness variation, residual stress, strain-layer fatigue, surface damage | Friction and lubrication control, pass schedule, tube quality, wall mapping, stress relief |
| CWR/skew rolling | Mannesmann cavities, surface hollows, spiral marks, backfin, ovality | Roll condition, mandrel design, controlled reduction, machine vision, positive machining allowance |
| Tube drawing/sinking | Inner wrinkles, polygonal bore, galling, residual stress, repeated-anneal distortion | Inner-tool support, surface treatment, drawing schedule, annealing and bore inspection |
| Hydroforming | Wrinkling, necking, cracking, leakage, local thinning | Pressure/axial-feed path, lubrication, material model, temperature and die control |
| Spinning/flow forming | Pass-to-pass thickness variation, cracking, springback, residual stress | Roller path, mandrel accuracy, moderate reduction, intermediate thermal control |
| Welding or press-fit | Porosity, incomplete consolidation, HAZ effects, fatigue at joint, runout | Friction-weld parameter control, joint NDT, post-weld machining, dynamic balancing |
| Additive | Porosity, lack of fusion, anisotropy, residual stress, rough bore | Qualified powder/process, CT or UT, stress relief, machining, fatigue and balance validation |

### 6.4 Heat-treatment distortion

Heat treatment can determine whether a near-net formed shaft remains economical. Carburizing offers hard spline or gear surfaces but can distort long hollow geometries and thin walls. Induction hardening is localized and can reduce the total thermal exposure, but the inductor must follow the geometry and avoid excessive case depth or uneven heating.

ZHY’s study of a stepped gear shaft found lower runout after carburizing 20CrMnTiH than after induction hardening of 42CrMoH or 40CrH. Segmented induction reduced distortion relative to one-shot induction, while deeper cases increased the percentage of parts requiring straightening. The same study found higher static torsional strength in induction-hardened 42CrMoH than in carburized 20CrMnTiH [ZHY induction-hardening study](https://www.zhygear.com/research-on-induction-hardening-technology-for-drive-cylindrical-gear-shaft/).

These results should not be generalized as “carburizing is more accurate” or “induction is stronger.” They show that:

- geometry and inductor design matter;
- case depth changes distortion;
- the material grade changes response;
- segmented induction can improve local control;
- final straightening and grinding must be included in the process plan.

A suitable shaft route should be selected together with the heat-treatment route. Choosing the forming method first and treating hardening as a later subcontracting detail can erase the expected material and machining savings.

### 6.5 Balance, inspection, and traceability

A production-quality shaft requires more than dimensional inspection. A representative control plan should include:

- certified steel chemistry and material condition;
- hardness before and after heat treatment;
- case depth and microstructure;
- outside and inside diameter;
- wall-thickness distribution;
- roundness, cylindricity, straightness, and total runout;
- spline or gear pitch, profile, flank hardness, and runout;
- surface roughness at bearing, seal, spline, and gear surfaces;
- magnetic-particle or eddy-current inspection for surface defects;
- ultrasonic or other volumetric inspection where internal damage is a risk;
- bore cleanliness and particulate limits where the shaft carries oil or coolant;
- dynamic balancing to the specified current ISO 21940 requirement;
- traceability from heat and blank through forming, heat treatment, machining, and final rotor assembly.

The T/ZJDJ specification provides an unusually concrete shaft-level example: k5 fits for shaft journals, p5 for iron-core seats, h7 for resolver seats, surface roughness Ra0.4 μm at oil-seal surfaces, Ra0.8 μm at bearing seats, Ra1.6 μm at iron-core seats and end faces, and Ra3.2 μm at spline flanks unless hardened finishing reduces it to Ra1.6 μm. It also requires magnetic-particle inspection to show no surface or near-surface cracks and one-to-one correspondence between plain-digit and QR traceability codes [T/ZJDJ 002-2022](https://ndls.cnis.ac.cn/standard/detail/1bf70fee23d908c4df27c754520158da).

The IMARC facility case reports run-at-rate validation, Cpk ≥1.67 on critical-to-quality features, automated CMM verification, and dynamic-balance certification of every rotor. These are facility-level quality practices, not proof of a particular hollow-shaft process, but they illustrate the maturity expected in a modern e-axle supply chain [IMARC e-axle facility](https://www.imarcengineering.com/case-study/electric-motor-and-e-axle-manufacturing-facility).

## 7. Comparative assessment of the principal routes

### 7.1 Main comparison matrix

| Route | Materials and geometry | Cost and scale | Downstream burden | Performance and risk | Overall NEV position |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cold/warm near-net forging | Low- to medium-alloy steels; simple to moderately complex hollow, stepped, flanged, or splined forms | High tooling; cold tooling especially expensive; strong high-volume economics | Turning, drilling or boring, spline/gear formation, heat treatment, grinding, balancing | Good repeatability and fiber flow; high force, formability, die wear, and heat-treatment distortion | Default for stable, high-volume designs |
| Semi-hot mandrel radial forging | 42CrMo4, 20MnCr5, 34MnB5 and related steels; bottle-shaped, stepped, internal contours | Automotive-scale equipment exists; economic value comes from avoiding bore machining | Finish turning, feature forming, heat treatment, grinding, balancing | Strong one-piece and hollow integration; damage, bore distortion, and mandrel/feed sensitivity | Best complex-monobloc candidate |
| Rotary swaging plus axial forming | Steel and selected aluminum/titanium/copper alloys; tubular variable-wall shafts and splines | Modular, automated, material-efficient; direct unit-cost data unavailable | Limited external machining but hardening, grinding, balance, and inspection remain | Good torsional strengthening; friction-driven wall variation and residual stress | Leading tube-based alternative |
| Spline/form extrusion | Low/medium-carbon and low-alloy steels, aluminum, copper; axial profiles on hollow blanks | Attractive at high volume and high repeatability; tooling cost and tool life must be quoted | Body and bearing machining; heat treatment and hard finishing | Accurate local profile and low waste; high force, formability and tool-load limits | Strong for simple compatible profiles |
| CWR/skew rolling | Steel and some aluminum hollow billets; stepped preforms | Potentially low force and good material utilization; equipment and tool-life uncertainty | Positive machining allowance, heat treatment, gear/spline work, balance | Internal cavities, surface hollows, ovality, tool wear | Conditional preform route |
| Seamless tube and drawing | Low/medium-alloy steel tubes; constant or moderately stepped hollow body | Established tube supply; repeated drawing, annealing, and inner finishing can be expensive | End thickening, swaging or forging, machining, spline/gear, heat treatment | Good seamless integrity if inner surface is controlled; wrinkles and grinding burden | Useful blank route, not universal complete route |
| Hydroforming | Ductile steel and aluminum tubes; stepped external profiles | High capital and tooling; potentially low material and assembly cost at high volume | End machining, feature forming, heat treatment, balancing | Uniform wall and complex shape; pressure, wrinkle, crack, and control risks | Pilot candidate for tube-compatible designs |
| Spinning/flow forming | Steel, aluminum, titanium, magnesium with suitable thermal control | Flexible and relatively low tooling; multi-pass cycle burden | End forming, machining, heat treatment, balance | Good surface and wall control potential; residual stress and thermal variation | Prototype or conditional serial route |
| Split/friction-welded hybrid | DOM or seamless tubes with forged steel ends; dissimilar materials possible with qualification | Low forming complexity; adds joining, inspection, and assembly | Weld machining, heat treatment, NDT, balancing | Flexible architecture; joint fatigue and runout risks | Conditional where monobloc forming is impractical |
| Machining from tube or bar | Broadest material and geometry freedom | High material removal and cycle cost; low tooling and excellent flexibility | Full machining plus heat treatment, grinding, balance | Easy to modify and qualify; poor material utilization and chip burden | Prototype, low volume, and fallback route |

### 7.2 What the matrix does—and does not prove

The matrix supports a conditional ranking, not a universal price list. The strongest production evidence is split across different source types:

- Fink reports forging as the dominant first-stage route in an internal global study and gives an implemented cold-forging-to-machining chain.
- GFM reports automotive-scale radial forging and a specific semi-hot hollow EV-shaft geometry concept.
- Felss and Profiroll report industrial tube-based rotor-shaft routes with integrated swaging, axial forming, or spline rolling.
- Kinefac reports high-rate spline extrusion and electric motor-shaft applications.
- CWR and rotary compression studies demonstrate technical feasibility, but their production economics and NEV qualification are incomplete.
- Hydroforming, spinning, additive, and several advanced extrusion variants have technical or industrial precedent but weak direct evidence for finished NEV rotor shafts.

The apparent disagreement between the 95% forging figure and the attractiveness claims for swaging, extrusion, and tube forming is therefore explainable. Fink’s statistic concerns a broad industrialized rotor-shaft population and an unspecified survey. Supplier sources describe particular shaft geometries for which a different route may be more efficient. A broad market share does not invalidate a geometry-specific alternative.

## 8. Recommended manufacturing routes

### 8.1 Ranked conditional recommendation

#### Rank 1: Near-net cold or warm forging for stable, high-volume steel shafts

This is the default route when the shaft has:

- a stable design;
- high annual volume;
- a predominantly axisymmetric body;
- compatible steel formability;
- limited internal undercuts;
- splines or features that can be formed or machined after the body is made;
- sufficient volume to amortize dedicated dies and automation.

A representative route is:

**20MnCr5 or 20CrMnTi tube/billet → cold or warm hollow forging and local upsetting → turning and drilling/boring → axial spline forming, broaching, or gear milling → carburizing/carbonitriding → hard finishing and grinding → balancing and inspection.**

A 42CrMo4/4140 version is also attractive, especially where the shaft body carries high combined bending and torsion. Because 42CrMo4 has higher flow stress than low-carbon case-hardening steel, warm or semi-hot forming, staged reductions, or pre-annealing may be more practical than a single cold stroke.

The route’s main advantages are production repeatability, established automotive tooling, good material utilization relative to machining from bar, and favorable fiber flow. Its main risks are high tooling cost, formability limits, bore control, die wear, and heat-treatment distortion. Fink’s implemented example starts with cold forging and proceeds through turning, drilling, axial spline forming, induction hardening, hard turning, grinding, marking, demagnetization, and inspection [Hirschvogel rotor-shaft paper](https://www.hirschvogel.com/fileadmin/user_upload/ATZlive_Paper_HIVO_Rotorshaft_klf_V6.pdf).

This route should be selected only after the supplier demonstrates the complete chain, not merely the as-forged shape.

#### Rank 2: Semi-hot mandrel radial forging for bottle-shaped or stepped monobloc shafts

This is the strongest conditional route when the design contains:

- several stepped internal diameters;
- a bottle-shaped internal contour;
- a single-side-closed end;
- a need to avoid extensive internal machining;
- high torque and fatigue requirements;
- a preference for a one-piece shaft rather than welded parts.

The route can be:

**seamless or flow-formed hollow blank → semi-hot mandrel radial forging at approximately 700–850°C → end forming or upsetting → turning and drilling as required → spline extrusion or axial forming → induction, carburizing, or Q&T treatment → hard turning/grinding → balance and inspection.**

GFM’s EV-specific process description and the TRR188 industrial monobloc-tubular-shaft chain make this the most compelling choice for complex hollow geometry. The recommendation remains conditional because the available sources do not provide target-specific unit cost, tolerance capability, balance, fatigue, tool life, or run-at-rate data.

The required validation should focus on:

- wall-thickness and bore concentricity;
- damage and void formation;
- mandrel life;
- deformation uniformity across steps;
- heat-treatment distortion;
- final rotor critical speed;
- spline and gear quality;
- fatigue under combined bending, torsion, and regenerative reversal.

#### Rank 3: Rotary swaging combined with axial forming or spline rolling for thin-walled tube shafts

This route becomes the leading alternative when the shaft is fundamentally tubular and benefits from load-oriented wall distribution or integrated axial features.

A representative chain is:

**drawn or seamless tube → rotary swaging for outer contour and local wall distribution → axial forming or helical-gear forming → end upsetting or flange forming → localized hardening → hard finishing → dynamic balancing.**

Felss provides the strongest industrially relevant process description, while Profiroll demonstrates a tube-based full-length involute spline concept. Tian et al. provide supporting mechanical evidence for 42CrMo rotary swaging, including improved torsional strength and fatigue life, but their test used a solid rod rather than a hollow motor shaft.

This route is particularly attractive when:

- wall thickness can be controlled within the required range;
- the shaft has long axial features;
- the process can eliminate substantial turning or boring;
- a seamless or drawn tube is available;
- the product family includes multiple diameters that can share a modular machine.

It is less attractive when the shaft has very thin walls, severe stepped internal geometry, or stringent bore concentricity without sufficient post-forming machining. Friction, die wear, and pass history must be controlled because thin tubes are more sensitive to wall-thickness variation.

#### Rank 4: Spline or form extrusion for simple, repeatable shaft geometries

Spline/form extrusion is a strong local-feature process for high-volume shafts with:

- straight or gently stepped geometry;
- compatible low- or medium-carbon steel;
- an axial internal or external spline;
- stable geometry;
- sufficient tool access and run-out space.

It can be integrated with a forged or tubular blank. It is especially attractive when the spline or profile would otherwise require broaching, hobbing, or extensive milling.

Kinefac’s industrial description supports high accuracy, low waste, high repeatability, and fast cycles, while the Current Science paper supplies a direct NEV motor-shaft composite-extrusion concept using 20MnCr5. The limitation is evidence strength: the supplier data do not provide a common NEV cost model, and the direct NEV study is simulation-based.

For a 42CrMo4 shaft, the route may require warm forming, annealed stock, staged reductions, or a separate radial or swaging preform. For 20MnCr5/20CrMnTi, cold or warm extrusion is more naturally aligned with carburized spline or gear requirements.

#### Rank 5: CWR or skew rolling followed by forging, extrusion, or machining

CWR should be considered when the shaft family has:

- multiple external steps;
- a hollow billet or mandrel-compatible bore;
- a need for high material utilization;
- production volume sufficient to justify dedicated rolls;
- tolerance allowance for final machining.

The most credible architecture is hybrid:

**hollow billet → mandrel CWR or three-tool skew rolling → hot extrusion or local forging of complex ends → spline/gear formation → heat treatment → finish machining.**

The route can reduce equipment force and energy, but the evidence also shows internal cavities, surface hollows, tool wear, and the continued need for machining allowance. It is an engineering-development candidate rather than the default NEV production route.

#### Rank 6: Seamless tube, flow forming, spinning, or hydroforming for tube-compatible shafts

These routes are appropriate when the shaft design is driven by a long thin-wall tube, low tooling flexibility, or an external contour that is difficult to obtain by bulk forging.

- Seamless tube and drawing are attractive for a clean, continuous hollow body but may incur high internal finishing cost.
- Flow forming and spinning are attractive for prototypes, variants, and difficult-to-form alloys but need thermal and pass control.
- Hydroforming is attractive for complex external contours and high-volume tubular structures but requires high capital and has limited direct motor-shaft evidence.

They should normally be paired with end forming, radial forging, swaging, spline rolling, or friction-welded forged ends.

#### Rank 7: Split or friction-welded construction when architecture justifies it

A split shaft can be selected when:

- the hollow body and end features require different forming methods;
- a monobloc die would be too complex;
- a thin tube can carry torque while forged ends carry bearings or gears;
- the product specification permits press-fit or friction-welded construction;
- joint inspection and balance are manageable.

It is not the default for a fatigue-critical high-speed rotor shaft because every joint introduces another source of runout, residual stress, fatigue initiation, and inspection burden. The NEV-specific split-shaft standard makes it a legitimate route, but qualification must include joint fatigue and rotor dynamics.

### 8.2 Prototype and low-volume alternatives

For prototypes, development vehicles, short product runs, or uncertain demand, the most practical routes are:

1. machining from seamless tube or bar;
2. open-die or mandrel forging followed by machining;
3. rotary compression or spinning for a representative hollow preform;
4. flexible radial forging with limited tooling;
5. additive manufacture for geometry experiments or internal-passage studies, followed by extensive finishing and testing.

Machining from tube is preferable to machining from a large solid bar when the tube quality, wall thickness, and bore concentricity are acceptable. It reduces chip volume and can provide a realistic hollow geometry for rotor-dynamics and fatigue prototypes.

However, a machined prototype from bar does not reproduce forged fiber flow or residual stress. FIA guidance therefore distinguishes between a hogout for approximate static performance and an open-die forged, blocker-forged, or production-tool prototype for more representative dynamic behavior [Forging Industry Association guide](https://www.forging.org/Common/Uploaded%20files/Design%20Engineering%20Center/Product%20Design%20Guide%20for%20Forging.pdf).

### 8.3 Decision rules by shaft geometry

| Shaft condition | Preferred route | Secondary route | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Straight or mildly stepped hollow body, stable high volume | Cold/warm forging or extrusion | Rotary swaging | High repeatability and low material waste |
| Bottle-shaped, stepped internal contour, monobloc requirement | Semi-hot mandrel radial forging | Radial forging plus spline extrusion | Controls bore contour and avoids extensive inner machining |
| Thin-walled tube with long axial or helical features | Rotary swaging plus axial forming/spline rolling | Flow forming or seamless tube plus rolling | Integrates wall distribution and torque features |
| Simple internal spline on compatible blank | Spline/form extrusion | Broaching or axial forming | High-rate, repeatable local profile |
| Complex stepped preform where force reduction matters | Mandrel CWR or skew rolling | Rotary compression | Lower modeled force and potential material savings |
| Tube-compatible external contour, large stable volume | Hydroforming | Flow forming or spinning | Complex outer geometry and uniform wall potential |
| Separate forged ends and thin tube | Friction-welded hybrid | Press-fit split structure | Reduces monobloc forming complexity |
| Prototype or rapidly changing variant | Machining from tube/bar | Open-die or mandrel forging | Low tooling and high flexibility |
| Unusual lightweight or cooling concept | Additive or hybrid prototype | Flow forming/hydroforming | Geometry exploration only until fatigue and balance are proven |

## 9. Evidence strength, assumptions, and validation priorities

### 9.1 Evidence strength

The evidence base supports different conclusions at different levels.

**Established production practice**

- forging, cold/warm/hot forming, and machining are established automotive technologies;
- radial forging is established at automotive scale, although the cited production totals are not EV-specific;
- rotary swaging, axial forming, spline rolling, tube manufacture, and friction welding have industrial equipment and supplier use cases;
- heat treatment, grinding, balancing, CMM inspection, and NDT are established downstream operations.

**Strong technical feasibility**

- semi-hot mandrel radial forging for hollow bottle-shaped shafts;
- radial forging plus spline extrusion for monobloc tubular shafts;
- cold or warm composite extrusion of 20MnCr5 NEV motor-shaft concepts;
- rotary compression of stepped hollow shafts;
- three-tool skew rolling of hollow S355 preforms;
- cold radial forging of 20CrMnTiH;
- tube spinning and hot rotary drawing.

**Conditional or emerging for this application**

- hydroforming and hot metal gas forming of motor shafts;
- flow forming and spinning of high-speed steel rotor shafts;
- CWR as a complete NEV shaft route;
- additive manufacture of finished high-speed hollow shafts;
- powder forging of hollow motor shafts;
- nested-tube friction-welded rotor shafts where joint fatigue is critical.

Supplier claims are valuable for equipment and process capability but are not independent comparative trials. Simulation and laboratory studies establish mechanisms, loads, and defect risks but do not prove production OEE, unit cost, balance, or field fatigue.

### 9.2 What remains unavailable

The following requested quantities cannot be stated defensibly from the supplied evidence:

- one validated target-program geometry and duty cycle;
- shaft-level annual production volume;
- common tooling cost across routes;
- comparable cycle time and OEE;
- scrap and tool-life distributions;
- numerical unit costs and break-even quantities;
- head-to-head fatigue and balance results for the same hollow shaft;
- statistical capability data tied to every candidate route;
- validated aluminum, titanium, magnesium, hydroformed, spun, or additively manufactured NEV shaft material windows.

These gaps do not prevent route selection, but they make the recommendation conditional. A route should not be rejected merely because a published cost is absent, nor should a supplier’s qualitative claim be converted into a numerical ranking.

### 9.3 Minimum qualification evidence for the selected route

Before production-tool release, the preferred route should demonstrate the following on the target geometry and material:

1. **Material and preform capability.** Chemical analysis, cleanliness, tube or billet dimensional variation, annealed or spheroidized condition, and forming-force margin.
2. **Forming integrity.** Bore and wall-thickness maps, external profile, straightness, runout, metallography, surface inspection, and internal NDT where appropriate.
3. **Fiber flow and damage.** Macroetch or equivalent flow characterization, void or crack evaluation, and correlation of forming simulation with measured shape and load.
4. **Heat treatment.** Hardness, case depth, microstructure, residual stress where relevant, distortion, and straightening percentage.
5. **Feature quality.** Spline or gear profile, pitch, flank hardness, surface finish, run-out, and engagement testing.
6. **Finishing and cleanliness.** Bearing and seal-seat roughness, bore cleanliness, particle limits for oil or coolant passages, and corrosion protection.
7. **Rotor dynamics.** Shaft-only and assembled-rotor balance, critical-speed measurement or validated modal analysis, overspeed testing, and vibration response.
8. **Mechanical durability.** Torsional overload, combined bending and torsional fatigue, thermal cycling, regenerative bidirectional loading, and, where relevant, coolant-pressure or leak testing.
9. **Production capability.** Run-at-rate, capability studies on critical dimensions, tool-life evidence, scrap and rework rates, traceability, and customer PPAP or equivalent approval.

FITGEN’s MRL 7 criteria provide a useful general maturity threshold: production-representative capability, approved materials, material availability, pilot-line run-at-rate capability, supplier-quality assessment, tooling and test-equipment development, and completed FMEA/DFMA [FITGEN D1.3](https://www.fitgen-project.eu/files/FITGEN_D1.3_Reliable%20and%20scalable%20design%20ready%20for%20mass%20manufacturing%20and%20dismantling.pdf).

## Closing judgment

For a conventional high-volume steel NEV hollow motor shaft, begin with near-net cold or warm forging and a deliberately integrated downstream chain. Move to semi-hot mandrel radial forging when the shaft has a complex stepped or bottle-shaped internal contour that would make boring expensive or weaken fiber flow. Choose rotary swaging with axial forming or spline rolling when a thin-walled tube and integrated axial features are central to the design. Use spline extrusion for simple, repeatable, high-volume profiles, and evaluate CWR, hydroforming, spinning, rotary compression, or split construction only when their specific geometric advantage outweighs the weaker direct qualification evidence.

The final choice should be made at the level of the complete process chain—not the forming operation alone—because the decisive cost and reliability variables are usually machining allowance, heat-treatment distortion, spline or gear formation, balance, inspection, and verified fatigue performance.
